title: Am I Cool With Teachers Asking AI to Pretend Its Me
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a reader’s ethical question about using AI to impersonate him for lesson plan feedback, Stuart works through four structured thoughts on the matter. He first reveals he has conducted the same experiment himself, then argues that the intellectual property concern is practically moot—AI was trained on the public internet without creator consent, and that process is already complete. He returns to his original motivations for writing: to deepen his own practice and to be useful to others. If AI personas built on his work continue to serve those goals for readers, he has no serious objection. The article closes with a candid acknowledgment of the economic harm AI-generated summaries and chatbots have inflicted on the creator economy by displacing the human web traffic that sustains independent educational writers.
points: The intellectual property concern about AI mimicking a creator is practically resolved: AI was already trained on publicly posted content without permission, and the debate about whether that was ethical is separate from whether users should avoid the resulting capability.

Stuart tested the AI-as-himself experiment and found the mimicry accurate without providing any links—the models had ingested enough of his public writing to reproduce his voice and thinking, demonstrating how completely creator work has been absorbed.

Stuart’s original motivations for writing—deepening his own practice and being helpful to others—remain the benchmark for whether AI-mediated use of his work is acceptable; if the use advances those goals, it is tolerated.
AI’s known limitations apply regardless of persona: it can only add to existing user understanding, it can be wrong, it can become a crutch, and it carries environmental costs.

The creator economy is materially harmed by AI overviews and chatbots: human traffic to independent educational websites has declined sharply as AI replaces direct internet research, reducing the revenue that sustains independent practitioner-writers.
quotes: Rick isn’t the first person I’ve heard of doing this because I’ve done it myself. Yep. I’ve asked AI to pretend it’s me and give me advice from my perspective.

asking AI to pretend it’s me doesn’t enact a theft of my intellectual property. That theft has already taken place. The most up-to-date AI chatbots — e.g., Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and so on — have all been trained on basically the entire internet.
I’m not worried about it from the intellectual property angle; I’m just one of millions of creators whose work has been used in this matter, absent our permission.

Nothing has helped my practice more than writing about it. And Rick’s message attests to the success of the second — my work has been helpful to him. My writing has done for Rick what the writing of others (e.g., Jim Burke, Mike Schmoker, Kelly Gallagher, Penny Kittle) has done for me: it has behaved like a mentor.

if asking AI to pretend it’s me can help you in your work as an educator, I have no real qualms with it. There are, of course, the general qualms that come with any use of AI: it can only add to the understanding you already have; it can be wrong, in all sorts of ways; it can quickly become a crutch; it has environmental costs.

These tools have taken their toll on the creator economy in that they’ve radically reduced web traffic to creator websites and the appertaining revenue such traffic provides creators with. I’ve seen bot traffic to the server my site is hosted on explode and human traffic dwindle.
